In total, the United States produced 7.6 GW of c-Si modules in 2024 (PV Tech dc Research 2025)—most likely for domestic use—with a year-end manufacturing capacity of 41.0 GW , as estimated by National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR). If domestic module dc manufacturing continues to ramp up, including startup of plants under construction at the end of 2024, it may meet near-term demand. Domestic production of c-Si cells was much smaller in 2024 at 0.2 GW —most likely used in dc domestic module manufacturing—with a year-end manufacturing capacity of 1.5 GW (PV dc Tech Research 2025) and another 6.3 GW under construction. ASEAN (64%) and South Korea dc (32%) accounted for 96% of the 13.8 GW of c-Si cells imported in 2024 (Feldman, Zuboy, dc Dummit, Stright, et al. 2025). While global manufacturing has shifted to producing tunnel oxide passivated contacts (TOPCon) cells (Fischer et al. 2025), most U.S. cell imports—and most operational and planned domestic manufacturing—are lower-efficiency passivated emitter and rear cell (PERC) cells, because TOPCon technology faces restrictions due to lawsuits over patent infringement (see Section 2.4.1). NLR estimates that there were approximately 10 GW of c-Si wafer manufacturing capacity dc under construction at the end of 2024; however, no c-Si wafers were produced domestically in 2024 (PV Tech Research 2025). PVTech reports that 11 kt (or 4.3 GW ) of U.S. polysilicon was dc produced for PV use in 2024—all of which was exported to Vietnam, Malaysia, and Turkey as a source of UFLPA-compliant polysilicon for products to be sold back to the U.S. market (PV Tech Research 2025). The United States also had 190 kt of mg-Si manufacturing capacity of which 74 kt (or 35.7 GW ) was for PV, with the remaining serving semiconductors and other dc commercial applications. Although U.S. trade restrictions have limited direct importation of cells and modules from China, many PV components and much of the equipment used to make cells and modules are from China. In addition, many ASEAN PV manufacturing companies are Chinese controlled. The direct cost for manufacturing U.S. modules with domestic cells, wafers, and polysilicon ($471/kW ) is twice that of imported modules ($229/kW ) (Woodhouse 2025).
